Midrash Tanchuma, Noach 1:1-2: “[These are the generations of Noah (Gen. 6:9).] May it please our master to instruct us concerning the number of transgressions for which women die during childbirth. Thus have our masters taught us: Women die during childbirth for failure to observe three duties decreed in the Torah.

These are: The duty with regard to menstruation, for it is written: And if a woman have an issue of her blood, she shall be in her impurity seven days (Lev. 15:25); the duty of the levy of dough, for it is written: Of the first of your dough ye shall set apart a cake for a gift (Num. 15:20); and the duty of lighting the Sabbath lights, for it is written: And call the Sabbath a delight (Isa. 58:13). If one chooses to sit in darkness, the Sabbath would not then be a delight, since darkness is imposed upon those condemned to Gehenna, as it says: A land of thick darkness, as darkness itself (Job 10:22).”

paragraphs.text: Peri Tzadik, Mishpatim 6:1: “But this is stated concerning Shabbat in the Sabbatical year because one might have thought that the essential commandment of Shabbat is for Israel to be free one day in seven for Torah and the service of God, blessed be He. During the working days, one turns to his olive grove and another to his vineyard, occupied with the affairs of this world; God, blessed be He, commanded them to rest from labor on Shabbat and be free for Torah. If so, in the Sabbatical year they had no such occupation throughout the year, since their principal work was working the land, and this was forbidden in the Sabbatical year. The poor and the rich were equal regarding the spontaneous growth, so the entire year was like Shabbat. Scripture therefore taught us that even in the seventh year the Shabbat of Creation is not displaced. Shabbat is similarly mentioned at the beginning of Ki Tisa and in Vayakhel, in the command to build the Tabernacle, to teach that its construction does not override Shabbat. One might have reasoned that, since throughout the week they were also occupied in causing the Divine Presence to dwell on earth, all the days were like Shabbat, and Shabbat would then be displaced. Scripture taught us that Shabbat is not overridden. For although being free for Torah and divine service is indeed part of Shabbat’s purpose, even when a person is free every day and occupied in Torah and divine service, Shabbat still has its own purpose: one merits holiness from God, blessed be He, which is fixed and enduring, as it is said, “To know that I am the Lord Who sanctifies you.””

paragraphs.text: Midrash Tanchuma, Bereshit 2:11: “In any event, we must learn whether one is permitted to complete a fast on a Friday. We might say it is forbidden to complete the fast, for then one would enter the Sabbath in a weakened condition; but, on the other hand, we might contend that it is permitted to complete the fast, since one would not be fasting on the Sabbath. Listen to what Rabba said concerning this matter: “When we were visiting R. Nahman one day, he propounded the question, ‘May students who fast on a Friday complete their fast; that is, may a person begin the observance of the Sabbath while in a weakened condition?’ We were not able to answer this query. When we came to the home of R. Judah, we asked him, and he was unable to answer. Rabba then said: ‘Let us consider this question in relation to the ninth day of Ab. If the ninth day of Ab occurs on a Friday, an unsalted, roasted egg may be brought and eaten, so that one might enter the Sabbath free from hunger.’””

paragraphs.text: Midrash Tanchuma, Bereshit 2:1: “An inquiry: The house of Israel is obligated to rest on the day of Shabbat. When the Holy One, blessed be He, created His world, He created it in six days and rested on the day of Shabbat; He blessed and sanctified it, like one who built a house, completed his work, and made a festive day. Thus people speak of a celebration upon completing a house, as it is written: “God completed on the seventh day.” The Merciful One says: Rest on the day of Shabbat, just as I rested on it, as it is written: “He rested on the seventh day; therefore the Lord blessed,” and so forth.”

Berakhot 33b:1-2: “There are conflicting opinions with regard to reciting havdala over the cup of wine after reciting it in the Amida prayer. One opinion holds that it is appropriate to recite havdala a second time, while the other holds that it is prohibited. Ravina said to Rava: What is the halakha? Rava said to him: The halakha in the case of havdala is like the halakha in the case of kiddush. Just as in the case of kiddush, although one recited kiddush in the Amida prayer he must, nevertheless, recite kiddush again over the cup of wine, so too with havdala, although one recited havdala in the Amida prayer he must recite havdala again over the cup of wine.

The mishna states that Rabbi Eliezer says: It is recited in the seventeenth blessing of the Amida prayer, the blessing of thanksgiving.”

paragraphs.text: Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 9:1: “What is in the heart is called a “secret,” for it cannot be revealed to another at all. As I heard: “secret” does not mean something that can be revealed in speech, since after it is revealed the other person knows it just as he does, and it is no secret at all. Rather, a “secret” is something that cannot be revealed in any way whatsoever. That is, the feeling of the light in the heart cannot be conveyed or explained at all to another who does not understand it in his own heart and feel it in this way.”

quotation.he: וזה שבלב הוא הנקרא "סוד", שזה אי אפשר לגלות לחברו כלל, כמו ששמעתי: ד"סוד" אין נקרא מה שאפשר לגלות בדבור, שאם כן אחר שיגלה גם האחר יודע כמוהו ואינו סוד כלל; רק "סוד" הוא מה שאי אפשר לגלותו כלל בשום אפן, שעל זה נאמר: "סוד ה' ליראיו" [תהלים כ״ה:י״ד], שידיעת השם יתברך סוד אצלם שאין יכולים לגלותו; והיינו דהרגשת האור בלב אי אפשר כלל להטעים ולהסביר לחברו שאינו מבין בלבו ומרגיש כך.
quotation.en: What is in the heart is called a “secret,” for it cannot be revealed to another at all. As I heard: “secret” does not mean something that can be revealed in speech, since after it is revealed the other person knows it just as he does, and it is no secret at all. Rather, a “secret” is something that cannot be revealed in any way whatsoever. Of this it is said, “The secret of the Lord is for those who fear Him” [Psalms 25:14]: their knowledge of God, blessed be He, is a secret that they cannot reveal. That is, the feeling of the light in the heart cannot be conveyed or explained at all to another who does not understand it in his own heart and feel it in this way.

paragraphs.text: Machshavot Charutz 8:1: “The question of divine knowledge and free choice is well known. It was answered in Zohar Chadash and in the Arizal’s book Arba Me’ot Shekel Kesef according to the esoteric teaching. The root of the matter is that they belong to two realms, and in the realm of divine knowledge there is truly no place for free choice. But this realm is concealed in this world and will be revealed in the future, when the evil inclination is removed and free choice is truly nullified. As stated in Shabbat (151b): “‘Years of which you will say, I have no desire in them’ (Ecclesiastes 12:1)—these are the days of the Messiah.” Then it will also become clear regarding all of Israel’s sins that they have been ordered and unfolding since the six days of Creation, as stated in the chapter Rabbi Akiva (Shabbat 89b). That is, divine knowledge will be revealed: everything was known to Him, blessed be He, from the beginning of Creation. In this world, however, is the realm of free choice.”

paragraphs.text: Resisei Layla 54:2: “In truth, a person’s chief effort lies in the service of the heart, as they said (Berakhot 33a): “What does the Lord your God ask of you, except to fear Him?” Fear is in the heart, as they said in Yoma (72b), concerning the verse (Proverbs 17:16), “but there is no heart”: this refers to a Torah scholar who has no fear of Heaven. Torah is the outwardly manifest service, and its essential source is Heaven, as they said in Megillah (6b): “To retain one’s learning requires assistance from Heaven.” They said in Niddah (16b) that at a person’s formation it is decreed whether he will be wise or foolish, meaning wise in Torah. Nevertheless, this too requires labor and effort. Indeed, most of the Torah’s commandments involve actual deeds; nevertheless, in all of them the decisive matter is the intention of the heart, and that is the essence of the service.”

paragraphs.text: Yisrael Kedoshim 6:1: “Every complete structure has ten levels, and its beginning from below is “Kingship is the mouth; we call it the Oral Torah” (Petaḥ Eliyahu). This is the root of the community of Israel, as Scripture says, “He has not done so for any nation” (Psalms 147:20). Chagigah (13a) derives from this that words of Torah are not handed over to a gentile. See Tosafot there, who found this difficult. In my view, the matter is straightforward: the precise expression is “handed over,” not “taught.” “Handed over” has the sense used at the beginning of Avot (chapter 1, mishnah 1): “He handed it over to Joshua.” Once Moses came and brought the Torah down to earth, it was entrusted to the sages of Israel. “It is not in heaven” (Deuteronomy 30:12), as they said in Bava Metzia (59b): they paid no heed to a heavenly voice for this reason, since the Torah had already been handed over to Israel, like something entrusted to another and placed in the recipient’s authority to act with it as he wishes. This is the Oral Torah that explains the Written Torah, for without the Oral Torah it is impossible to understand any commandment accurately at all. It was entrusted to the sages of Israel, and everything that a seasoned disciple will one day bring forth anew is Oral Torah. It distinguishes Israel from the nations, as stated at the beginning of Shemot Rabbah, chapter 47, section 1; see there.”

This is like the exposition (Berakhot 32b) of “And I will not forget you”: this refers to the event at Sinai. “I am” is the root of all words of Torah, as Shir HaShirim Rabbah says on “Let him kiss me”: when they heard the utterance “I am,” Torah learning became fixed in their hearts; see there. “Anokhi” contains the letter kaf, signifying keter, “crown,” and also the letters of ayin, “nothingness,” as the Zohar states (III 256b). Thus “And I”—the utterance “I am,” corresponding to the supreme crown, which is the crown of kingship—“will surely conceal”: it will be concealed. For the Oral Torah is concealed: it seems to the sages that their new teachings arise from their own intellect, yet they are the words of the living God, dripping from the dew of the Ancient One into the hearts of the sages of Israel.”

paragraphs.text: Peri Tzadik, Purim 1:2: “The letters yod-heh form a divine Name on their own, alluding to wisdom and understanding, the mind and the heart. A person can merit this union: the joining of wisdom in the mind with understanding and the will in the heart. But the essential task is to unite the Name yod-heh with vav-heh, so that the union is with the community of Israel. The letters vav-heh allude to Torah and commandments, as the holy Zohar explains (Naso, beginning of 123b). Therefore vav-heh on their own do not constitute a divine Name, for wisdom and understanding are the hidden dimensions in mind and heart, in love and fear; Torah without fear and love does not ascend, as Tikkunei Zohar states (Tikkun 10). The essential union is to merit the union of yod-heh with vav-heh, which is not constant: the union of wisdom and understanding, mind and heart, with the actual practice of Torah and commandments. This union cannot be complete so long as the descendants of Amalek remain—that is, so long as Amalek has any existence. Amalek is the evil inclination, as the holy Zohar explains concerning “Amalek dwells in the land of the Negev,” and it can enter even the hearts of great and holy people (as explained in Parashat Zakhor, discourse 1; see there at length). Therefore, after Amalek was blotted out, “The Jews had light,” and so forth: four things corresponding to the four letters of the divine Name.”

paragraphs.text: Peri Tzadik, Vayechi 10:1: “Even the other prophets, who looked through a mirror that was not clear, nevertheless received a prophetic vision shown to them from Heaven. For this reason they too could not see what Rabbi Akiva’s eyes saw. He did not see through a prophetic vision, but through wisdom flowing from the dew of the Ancient One; he could therefore apprehend more of the root that is concealed in this world. Hence they said of him, “His eye saw every precious thing.” “Preciousness” is the Aramaic equivalent of “glory,” for he could apprehend all of God’s glory, though not by sight—“My face shall not be seen”—but through the understanding of wisdom. This resembles the difference between an Aramaic translation and the holy tongue. The holy tongue is the very sacred speech of the blessed God in His Torah, with which He created His world. A translation is the understanding of that same matter, rather than the thing itself. Likewise, Moses’ vision was the thing itself, while Rabbi Akiva’s seeing was the eye of wisdom: through understanding he apprehended every precious thing.”

paragraphs.text: Jerusalem Talmud Demai 4:1:1-2: “One who buys produce from someone who is not trustworthy concerning tithes, and forgets to tithe it, asks him on Shabbat and may eat on his word. Once it becomes dark after Shabbat, he may not eat until he tithes. … Rabbi Bibi said in the name of Rabbi Chanina: The awe of Shabbat rests upon him, and he tells the truth. If the awe of Shabbat rests upon him, how can we have learned: “Once it becomes dark after Shabbat, he may not eat until he tithes”? Because of someone upon whom the awe of Shabbat does not rest.”

quotation.en: One who buys produce from someone who is not trustworthy concerning tithes, and forgets to tithe it, asks him on Shabbat and may eat on his word. Once it becomes dark after Shabbat, he may not eat until he tithes. … Rabbi Bibi said in the name of Rabbi Chanina: The awe of Shabbat rests upon him, and he tells the truth. If the awe of Shabbat rests upon him, how can we have learned: “Once it becomes dark after Shabbat, he may not eat until he tithes”? Because of someone upon whom the awe of Shabbat does not rest.

paragraphs.text: Meiri on Shabbat 118b:1: “In the Jerusalem Talmud they said: With what does one delight in it? One authority said: with sleep; another said: with Torah study. They do not disagree: one refers to a student, the other to a householder. My teachers explained that the student delights in it through Torah study, and the householder through sleep. I say the opposite: a student who studies all the days of the week fulfills Shabbat delight through sleep, so that his mind will not become excessively weary. But a householder who attends to his affairs throughout the weekdays should spend some time on Shabbat studying Torah as a form of delight.”

paragraphs.text: Shabbat 54b: ‘The Gemara raises an objection: Wasn’t it taught in a baraita: This is only permitted provided that he raises the rope one handbreadth from the ground? Apparently, there is no restriction with regard to the length of rope that may hang below the person’s hand. The Gemara answers: When this baraita was taught, it was taught with regard to the length of rope between the camel and the person holding it. That part of the rope may not sag to the ground; rather, it must be raised at least one handbreadth so that it is clear that the rope is attached to the camel. MISHNA: This mishna lists additional objects with which an animal may not go out into the public domain on Shabbat: A donkey may neither go out with the saddlecloth when it is not tied to its back, nor with a bell even if it is plugged to prevent it from ringing, nor with a ladder that is around its neck, nor with a strap that is around its leg. And the roosters may not go out with strings and not with a strap on their feet, which are tied there as a sign of ownership. And the rams may not go out with a small wagon under their tails, as it was common practice to put a small wagon under the tails of grown sheep so that the tail would not be injured by dragging on the ground. And ewes may not go out ḥanunot, nor may a calf go out with a gimon, nor may a cow go out with the skin of a hedgehog [kupar], nor with a strap between its horns. The mishna relates that Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya’s cow would go out on Shabbat with a strap between its horns, contrary to the will of the Sages. GEMARA: We learned in the mishna that a donkey may not go out on Shabbat with a saddlecloth if it was not tied to its back. The Gemara explains: What is the reason? As we stated above, there is room for concern that when not secured, the saddlecloth is liable to fall off the animal’s back, and its owner may come to retrieve the saddlecloth in the public domain. We also learned in the mishna: A donkey may not go out with a bell even if it is plugged to prevent it from ringing. The reason is that the animal’s owner appears like one going to the market, who adorns his donkey with bells in honor of market day.’

paragraphs.text: Shabbat 54b:18-19: “Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah’s cow: Did he have only one cow? Did Rav not say—and some say that Rav Yehudah said in Rav’s name—that Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah used to tithe twelve thousand calves from his herd each and every year? It was taught: It was not his; it belonged to his female neighbor. Because he did not protest to her, it was called by his name.”
